items.prompt: A stateless EC2 fleet has request load proportional to CPU and a stable warm-up time. Which scaling policy is a candidate?
constraints: The fleet is behind a load balancer.

options.text: Evaluate target tracking on average CPU or a validated load metric, with minimum, maximum, warm-up, cooldown, and health settings tested.
Scale only after CPU reaches 100 percent.
Set maximum capacity equal to current capacity.
Scale from log count without validating its relationship to work.

feedback.Reason: Target tracking fits a stable utilization signal when capacity and warm-up are correctly bounded.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Auto Scaling target tracking adjusts desired capacity toward a target metric value within configured bounds.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner validates CPU-to-latency correlation, warm-up, scale-in protection, and spare capacity under load.
Details.errorCorrection: Waiting for 100 percent causes SLO failure, fixed maximum prevents scale-out, and an unvalidated log signal is unreliable.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Target tracking simplifies policy but can lag if the metric is not leading or warm-up is misconfigured.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Scaling must begin before hard saturation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Maximum capacity must leave room for expected peaks.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A metric needs workload correlation before controlling capacity.

items.prompt: An API fleet has low and variable CPU because requests spend time waiting on I/O. Which metric is more useful for scaling?
constraints: Request count per target is available.

options.text: Evaluate request count per target or concurrency as the scaling signal, and validate it against latency, task capacity, and downstream quotas.
Use CPU only because API capacity is always CPU-bound.
Scale on total instance count without measuring demand.
Use error count as the normal leading signal when errors are already the SLO breach.

feedback.Reason: Per-target request or concurrency metrics can represent useful work when CPU is not predictive.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Load-balancer request metrics and application concurrency can map demand to fleet capacity more directly than host CPU.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect tests target values, startup delay, connection pools, and scale-in behavior against p99 latency.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU can be low at I/O wait, total count is not demand, and error count reacts after failure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Request metrics need correct target registration and can be distorted by uneven request cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU is not the measured demand signal in an I/O-bound service.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity count without demand cannot drive scaling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Errors are a late and harmful trigger for normal scale-out.

items.prompt: A worker fleet consumes messages and CPU varies with message type, while queue age predicts user delay. Which trigger is appropriate?

options.text: Scale from queue depth or age per worker, with visibility timeout, worker startup, maximum capacity, and downstream limits modeled.
Scale from CPU only even when message cost varies widely.
Scale from queue length without dividing by worker capacity or measuring age.
Delete old messages to keep queue depth low.

feedback.Reason: Queue age or normalized depth directly expresses backlog and user delay for worker systems.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backlog per worker and message age estimate how much work each consumer must process and when it will complete.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets target backlog, capacity bounds, visibility timeout, retries, and DLQ behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU is not consistent across message types, raw length ignores worker capacity, and deletion loses work.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Aggressive scale-out reduces age but can overload downstream services and increase cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Variable message cost breaks CPU as a stable demand signal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Queue length needs capacity and processing-time context.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting messages is data loss, not scaling.

items.prompt: A fleet must add capacity quickly when utilization crosses several thresholds and remove it cautiously. Which policy should be compared?
constraints: The metric has meaningful threshold bands.
Scale-out and scale-in have different risk.

options.text: Evaluate step scaling with separate adjustments and cooldown or warm-up behavior for scale-out and scale-in, then test oscillation and recovery.
Use one fixed adjustment for every metric value.
Scale in aggressively at the first low sample.
Add capacity only after the highest threshold is breached.

feedback.Reason: Step scaling maps different breach magnitudes to different capacity adjustments and can separate scale directions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Step policies use alarm breach size and configured adjustments to change desired capacity.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models warm-up, metric noise, cooldown, and minimum capacity and tests burst and recovery cases.
Details.errorCorrection: One adjustment may be too slow or too large, early scale-in causes thrash, and latest-only scale-out is late.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Step policies offer control but require more threshold tuning than target tracking.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Different overload magnitude can require different capacity responses.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Scale-in should be conservative and stable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Waiting for the highest threshold sacrifices response time.

items.prompt: A retail fleet has predictable daily peaks and a known warm-up time. Which scaling control should be evaluated?

options.text: Use scheduled scaling to add baseline capacity before the peak and combine it with reactive scaling for forecast error or unexpected demand.
Use reactive scaling only after requests begin failing.
Keep maximum capacity all day without cost review.
Disable scale-in after the peak permanently.

feedback.Reason: Scheduled scaling uses known demand timing to cover startup delay before reactive metrics rise.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Auto Scaling scheduled actions change capacity at a configured time, while dynamic policies handle residual demand.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner schedules a measured baseline, leaves headroom for forecast error, and verifies post-peak scale-in.
Details.errorCorrection: Failure-driven scale-out is late, maximum all-day capacity wastes cost, and permanent scale-in disablement leaks resources.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Scheduled capacity depends on forecast accuracy and time-zone or calendar maintenance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Reactive scaling cannot remove known startup delay before a peak.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A maximum fleet all day is not cost-efficient.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Scale-in protection should be bounded and reviewed.

items.prompt: A workload has repeatable weekly demand and several minutes of instance startup. Which approach may reduce reactive lag?
constraints: The fleet can use predictive or scheduled capacity.

options.text: Evaluate predictive or scheduled scaling with a reactive safety policy, validating forecast error, warm-up, minimum capacity, and cost.
Remove reactive scaling because forecasts are always exact.
Scale only on yesterday's peak without observing current demand.
Use error rate as the forecast input without checking traffic volume.

feedback.Reason: Forecast-based capacity can cover predictable demand ahead of time but needs reactive protection for error.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Predictive scaling uses historical metrics or forecasts, while dynamic policies correct deviations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner backtests forecasts, sets a safety floor and ceiling, and monitors under- and over-provisioning.
Details.errorCorrection: Forecasts are uncertain, yesterday's peak may not match current demand, and errors are a late indirect signal.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Predictive capacity lowers startup latency but can waste resources when demand changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Forecast error requires a reactive safeguard.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Historical peaks are not a current demand measurement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Error rate does not forecast healthy workload volume reliably.

items.prompt: Average latency is healthy but p99 latency violates the user SLO during bursts. Which scaling signal should be evaluated?

options.text: Use a validated p95 or p99 latency, concurrency, or queue metric as a leading signal and correlate it with capacity and downstream saturation.
Keep scaling from average latency because tails do not affect users.
Scale after timeout count reaches the SLO budget.
Increase timeout so p99 no longer appears as an error.

feedback.Reason: Tail latency is a user-facing signal and average values can hide the overload causing it.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Percentile metrics reveal distribution tails; scaling and dependency telemetry identify whether extra capacity can reduce them.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner uses a stable percentile or leading concurrency metric and tests noise, sampling, and scale delay.
Details.errorCorrection: Averages can mask p99, timeout counts are late, and increasing timeout hides failure rather than improving latency.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tail metrics can be noisy and need enough sample volume and careful aggregation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Tail latency is the stated user objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Timeouts are a late signal after the SLO has failed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A larger timeout does not reduce actual latency.

items.prompt: A fleet's 5xx rate rises during a dependency outage, but adding instances cannot repair the dependency. What scaling rule is safer?
constraints: The dependency is the measured bottleneck.
A circuit breaker or load shedding path exists.

options.text: Do not use raw errors as an unconditional scale-out trigger; protect the dependency with circuit breaking, bounded retries, load shedding, and a metric that indicates recoverable demand.
Scale without limit on every 5xx response.
Retry each failed request more times to create useful work.
Hide the errors from monitoring so scaling remains stable.

feedback.Reason: Errors can indicate a dependency failure where more compute creates a retry storm instead of recovery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Scaling signals must distinguish capacity saturation from non-capacity failure and protect downstream services.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner uses dependency health, queueing, and saturation signals with bounded retries and visible degraded behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Unbounded scale and retries amplify load, and hiding errors removes the diagnosis path.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Load shedding protects the system but can reduce immediate success and needs product policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Infinite scale cannot fix an unavailable dependency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Retries multiply failed work and can worsen the outage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Monitoring must expose the failure for safe operation.

items.prompt: A multi-tenant service has different request costs by tenant and aggregate CPU hides a noisy tenant. What metric design is needed?

options.text: Emit a bounded service or workload metric that represents useful work and isolate noisy tenants through quotas or capacity partitions rather than unbounded high-cardinality autoscaling.
Create one autoscaling policy per tenant without a cardinality or quota plan.
Scale from total request count without weighting request cost.
Ignore tenant identity because aggregate CPU is sufficient by definition.

feedback.Reason: A useful scaling metric must reflect heterogeneous work without creating unmanageable metric dimensions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Custom CloudWatch metrics can represent workload units, but cardinality, isolation, and quota boundaries affect operability.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses bounded dimensions, sets tenant quotas, and validates scale response and fairness.
Details.errorCorrection: Per-tenant policies can explode operations, raw count ignores work cost, and aggregate CPU hides noisy behavior.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More precise metrics need instrumentation and governance to avoid metric cost and control-plane complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unbounded policies and dimensions create operational and quota risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Equal request counts can represent very different work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Aggregate CPU is not sufficient when tenants have different resource profiles.

items.prompt: An autoscaling policy repeatedly adds and removes capacity during noisy metric changes. What should be adjusted?
constraints: Scale actions have a measurable warm-up.

options.text: Review metric period, aggregation, target, cooldown or warm-up, scale-in protection, and adjustment size, then test oscillation under representative traffic.
Shorten every evaluation period and make both directions aggressive.
Disable scale-in forever.
Ignore oscillation because each action is individually valid.

feedback.Reason: Scaling control needs enough signal stability and action delay to avoid reacting to its own changes.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Metric noise, warm-up, cooldown, and scale-in protection influence feedback-loop stability.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tunes periods and thresholds, separates scale directions, and verifies cost and SLO during bursts and recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: Aggressive bidirectional actions amplify thrash, permanent scale-in disablement leaks cost, and local validity can still produce an unstable loop.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Smoother response may react slower, so thresholds must retain enough capacity margin.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Shorter and more aggressive actions can amplify noise.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Permanent scale-in disablement is not a balanced policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Feedback stability is a system property, not only an individual action property.

items.prompt: A new instance takes four minutes to become healthy, but the scaling policy assumes one-minute warm-up. What is the risk?
constraints: The policy uses estimated instance warm-up.

options.text: Set warm-up and cooldown from measured bootstrap, image, health-check, and traffic readiness time, then verify the policy does not under-scale or overreact.
Set warm-up to zero so Auto Scaling launches continuously.
Lower maximum capacity because startup is slow.
Count an instance as capacity before it can serve healthy traffic.

feedback.Reason: Autoscaling must know when new capacity is actually contributing to service, not merely launched.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Instance warm-up influences how scaling policies interpret capacity and issue subsequent actions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures readiness, aligns health checks and warm-up, and tests burst and failure scenarios.
Details.errorCorrection: Zero warm-up causes policy overshoot or misleading capacity, lower max worsens shortage, and unready instances cannot serve users.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long warm-up slows policy reaction but avoids repeated over-launch and false capacity assumptions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Zero warm-up makes new but unready instances look like capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Slow startup requires more planning, not less maximum capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Capacity should be counted when it is healthy and serving.

items.prompt: A fleet has a maximum capacity equal to its normal peak but must survive an AZ loss. What capacity setting should be reviewed?
constraints: The service has a latency SLO.

options.text: Set minimum, desired, and maximum capacity from normal demand plus failure headroom and scale-out time, then test loss of one AZ.
Keep maximum at normal peak because an AZ loss cannot affect a multi-AZ fleet.
Set minimum to zero for a production low-latency service.
Disable rebalance and health replacement during the AZ event.

feedback.Reason: Multi-AZ placement does not remove the capacity loss from an AZ event; maximum and minimum must include recovery margin.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Auto Scaling desired and maximum limits bound how much capacity can be restored after a failure.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models N+1 or equivalent capacity and validates health replacement and scale-out time.
Details.errorCorrection: An AZ loss reduces fleet capacity, zero minimum is unsafe for low latency, and disabling replacement prolongs failure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Failure headroom costs more but is part of the availability target.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Multi-AZ improves placement but does not preserve capacity automatically.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Scale-from-zero cannot meet an immediate production SLO.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health replacement is needed during failure recovery.

items.prompt: A single metric cannot distinguish high traffic from a downstream outage. What alarm design helps operators?
constraints: Traffic, latency, and dependency health are available.
A scaling action must not worsen outages.

options.text: Use separate alarms and composite operational signals for demand, saturation, dependency health, and SLO, while keeping scaling triggers focused on recoverable capacity pressure.
Combine every metric into one opaque threshold.
Scale on dependency error alone.
Suppress dependency alarms during high traffic.

feedback.Reason: Operational alarms should preserve causal signals and avoid turning dependency failure into blind scale-out.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch alarms can combine or correlate metrics, but scaling and notification logic should remain explainable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner separates demand, saturation, and dependency failure paths and tests alarm state transitions.
Details.errorCorrection: Opaque thresholds hide cause, dependency errors can trigger a retry storm, and suppressing alarms removes safety evidence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More alarms require ownership and tuning but improve response quality.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Opaque aggregation makes diagnosis and policy behavior hard to verify.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Dependency errors may not be fixed by more compute.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: High traffic is when dependency failures are most important to see.

items.prompt: A workload has seasonal baselines and a sudden change can indicate either a product event or a failure. Which CloudWatch capability should complement fixed thresholds?
constraints: Operators need an anomaly indicator, not blind automation.

options.text: Evaluate anomaly detection or forecast-aware analysis alongside fixed SLO and capacity thresholds, with human review before high-impact scaling changes.
Replace all SLO alarms with anomaly bands.
Treat every anomaly as a request to double capacity.
Disable historical metrics to avoid false positives.

feedback.Reason: Anomaly detection can add context for changing baselines but does not replace explicit SLO and capacity controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch anomaly bands model expected metric behavior from history; fixed alarms remain useful for hard objectives.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner backtests bands, keeps deterministic safety thresholds, and validates any automated response against demand and dependency health.
Details.errorCorrection: Anomaly models can be wrong, every anomaly does not require double capacity, and history is required to learn baselines.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Adaptive detection reduces manual seasonal thresholds but needs enough history and careful action policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SLO and hard capacity limits remain explicit safety controls.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Anomaly magnitude does not directly map to capacity need.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Historical data enables anomaly detection and trend review.

items.prompt: A workload changes materially within one minute and requires a fast response. What metric design should be compared?
constraints: The scaling action has a short effective delay.
The extra metric cost is acceptable.

options.text: Evaluate high-resolution custom metrics only if their sampling, alarm, action, and startup latency materially improve the SLO, then compare cost and noise.
Use high-resolution metrics for every workload regardless of action delay.
Sample more frequently without changing the scaling policy or capacity warm-up.
Use one-minute data as proof of sub-second control response.

feedback.Reason: Higher-resolution metrics help only when the control loop and capacity response can use the extra signal.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch high-resolution custom metrics and alarms have different periods and pricing, while instance or task startup still creates delay.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures end-to-end control latency and uses the fastest useful signal rather than equating sampling with action speed.
Details.errorCorrection: High resolution adds cost and noise, sampling alone does not change policy or startup, and one-minute data cannot prove sub-second response.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fast telemetry increases cost and tuning effort and may cause oscillation if not filtered.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Resolution should be justified by the control-loop SLO.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Sampling alone does not change capacity action or warm-up.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Metric period is not the same as end-to-end response time.

items.prompt: A scale-in action can terminate instances holding long-running jobs. Which control should be configured?
constraints: Jobs have a finite completion time.
Instances can be protected or drained.

options.text: Use scale-in protection, lifecycle hooks, graceful draining, or a job-aware termination policy and verify that protection cannot block recovery forever.
Terminate the oldest instance immediately on every scale-in.
Disable scale-in permanently.
Ignore job state because Auto Scaling sees only instance health.

feedback.Reason: Scale-in must respect application work while retaining an escape path for unhealthy or stuck instances.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks, termination policies, and instance protection can coordinate replacement with application state.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner drains work, clears protection on completion, and alarms on protection age and capacity shortage.
Details.errorCorrection: Immediate termination loses work, permanent protection leaks cost, and instance health alone misses job state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Graceful scale-in slows cost reduction but preserves work and correctness.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Oldest is not necessarily safe to terminate while it holds work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Permanent disablement prevents elasticity and increases cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Application work state must be included in termination behavior.

items.prompt: An autoscaling plan can reach account quotas before the configured maximum. What should be visible in the design?

options.text: Compare desired maximum with service quotas, request increases where supported, reserve headroom for replacements, and alarm before the quota boundary.
Set maximum above the quota because Auto Scaling can bypass it.
Ignore quota alarms until scale-out fails.
Delete capacity reservations to make quota limits disappear.

feedback.Reason: Service quotas can cap elasticity independently of policy settings and need capacity planning.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Auto Scaling, EC2, ENI, IP, and instance quotas limit how much capacity can launch.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner audits quota usage, requests increases early, and tests the failure path before peak.
Details.errorCorrection: Policies cannot bypass quotas, failure-only detection is late, and reservations or capacity planning are separate decisions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Quota headroom and increases may require cost or governance work but protect scale-out.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Maximum capacity cannot exceed a hard service quota.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Quota failure leaves no scale-out response margin.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Reservations do not remove all relevant service quotas.

items.prompt: A service has a latency SLO and scaling from average utilization is too slow during short incidents. What additional signal can help operations?
constraints: SLO and request metrics are available.
The service can shed or queue work.
Scaling should not hide a dependency outage.

options.text: Use SLO or error-budget burn as an operational alarm alongside demand and saturation metrics, while keeping scale actions bounded and dependency-aware.
Scale without limit whenever any SLO violation occurs.
Suppress SLO alarms after scaling begins.
Use burn rate as proof that more instances always solve the problem.

feedback.Reason: SLO burn is valuable for alerting and prioritization, but it does not prove that compute is the cause.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SLO and error-budget signals express user impact; saturation and dependency signals identify recoverable capacity pressure.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner pages operators or triggers bounded mitigation and separately verifies whether capacity, dependency, or code caused the burn.
Details.errorCorrection: Unlimited scale can worsen an outage, suppressing alarms removes the signal, and more instances cannot fix every cause.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Burn-rate alerts can be sensitive and need multiple windows or human response policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SLO violation is not proof of compute shortage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Scaling does not make user impact disappear immediately.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Dependency and code failures may be unaffected by capacity.

items.prompt: A scaling alarm receives missing metrics during an agent or network failure. What should the policy decide explicitly?
constraints: A wrong state can scale or stop capacity.

options.text: Choose missing-data treatment from the failure risk, alarm semantics, and capacity safety requirement, and alert separately when the metric pipeline is unhealthy.
Treat missing data as healthy for every production service.
Treat missing data as a scale-out command without checking cause.
Ignore metric pipeline health because scaling is managed.

feedback.Reason: A missing metric is an observability failure and needs an explicit safe interpretation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch alarm missing-data treatment can change alarm state; metric pipeline failure may otherwise hide saturation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner selects conservative behavior, alarms on telemetry gaps, and tests the service during agent or network loss.
Details.errorCorrection: Healthy treatment can hide overload, automatic scale-out may worsen a network outage, and managed scaling still depends on customer metrics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Conservative capacity protects availability but can cost more during telemetry failure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Healthy is not universally safe when the service may be saturated.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Missing data does not identify a capacity cause.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Metric health is part of the scaling control loop.

items.prompt: A team proposes a custom metric and high-frequency polling to reduce scale latency. What should the design review include?
constraints: Metric and API charges are measurable.

options.text: Compare telemetry and control-plane cost, metric quality, action latency, capacity warm-up, false positives, and useful SLO improvement before adopting it.
Use the most frequent metric period because faster sampling always improves SLO.
Ignore false positives because extra capacity is harmless.
Increase metric frequency without changing the application demand signal.

feedback.Reason: A faster control loop is valuable only if it improves useful response after cost and noise are included.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Metric resolution, alarm evaluation, scaling action, and instance startup form a complete control latency chain.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner runs a before-and-after experiment and keeps the simplest signal that meets the SLO.
Details.errorCorrection: Faster sampling can add cost and noise, false positives create waste, and frequency does not repair a bad signal.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher resolution may be justified for rapid workloads but needs disciplined cardinality and thresholds.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Sampling speed is not the same as capacity readiness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: False positives can exhaust budget or quotas.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: More samples of an unrelated signal do not improve scaling.

items.prompt: A scaling policy looks correct from a diagram but has never been tested during dependency degradation or capacity shortage. What is missing?
constraints: The service has a failure objective.
A test environment or controlled drill exists.

options.text: Rehearse burst, slow startup, dependency throttling, quota exhaustion, unhealthy capacity, scale-in, and rollback, then record observed SLO and cost behavior.
Treat the policy document as proof of production behavior.
Test only normal steady-state CPU.
Disable scaling during drills so the baseline stays clean.

feedback.Reason: Scaling is a feedback system whose failure behavior must be observed under stress and dependency limits.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Policies interact with metrics, warm-up, quotas, health checks, and dependencies in ways a static diagram cannot prove.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner runs controlled load and fault tests, tunes thresholds, and keeps evidence for the release decision.
Details.errorCorrection: Documentation cannot validate timing, normal CPU is insufficient, and disabling control removes the behavior under test.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Rehearsal takes engineering time but avoids discovering a control-loop failure in production.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A diagram cannot prove runtime timing or failure behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Steady state omits bursts, outages, and quota boundaries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The drill must exercise the real control path to be useful.

items.prompt: A capacity review selects triggers from CPU, memory, queue, request count, latency, errors, and throughput without stating the decisive workload constraint. What should be fixed?
constraints: The service has an explicit SLO.
Scaling and failure behavior are part of the design.

options.text: Identify the resource or queue that predicts useful capacity and SLO breach, choose a leading metric, set safe bounds and warm-up, and verify with load and failure tests.
Use all metrics as equal triggers so every signal can scale capacity.
Choose CPU as the universal trigger for every service.
Choose the metric with the highest current value without workload analysis.

feedback.Reason: A scaling policy needs one or a deliberate set of causally relevant signals tied to capacity and SLO.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Different workload bottlenecks require different leading metrics, while multiple uncontrolled triggers can create conflicting actions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect profiles the path, defines thresholds and quotas, and validates scale-out, scale-in, and degraded states.
Details.errorCorrection: Equal triggers can oscillate or over-scale, CPU is not universal, and current magnitude without causality is not a design basis.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A composite policy can add resilience but must remain explainable and testable.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Every metric is not an independent capacity command.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Services can be I/O, queue, memory, dependency, or latency bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Current value does not establish what capacity would improve.
